lead: A cyber-physical system (CPS) joins computation with a physical process in a closed feedback loop. Sensors measure the process, a controller computes a command, and actuators change the process. The physical result depends on timing: the sampling period, actuator delay and sensor error all enter the loop. CPS ideas appear in engine ignition, anti-lock brakes, adaptive cruise control, drones, mobile robots and camera dollies. This chapter shows the loop and the errors that matter. Some syllabi call these mechatronics and IoT case studies.
prereq: You need: Unit 2 sensors and actuators; Unit 4 interfacing; and Unit 3 industrial protocols for plant examples (see Industrial IoT).

sections.h3: The closed loop and its timing

blocks.text: A CPS repeats four actions: measure the physical state, compute a command, drive an actuator, and let the process change. The next measurement closes the loop. A car brake, a robot wheel and a drone rotor are all physical processes here. The controller is a computer, but the result is physical. Timing is part of correctness: a command that arrives late is a wrong command.

blocks.where: f<sub>s</sub> is the sampling frequency in hertz (Hz); T<sub>s</sub> is the sampling period in seconds (s).

blocks.text: Sensor error is measured value minus true value. Actuator delay is the time from the command to the physical effect. These are separate faults. Slow sampling misses a fast change; actuator delay makes the correction late; sensor error makes the correction wrong.
A CPS is not just a sensor on the internet. The controller must act inside the process time scale. If the plant is a brake, the loop time is milliseconds; if it is a water tank, it may be seconds.

Electronic ignition uses a crank-angle sensor to time the spark. The engine control unit samples crank position, computes ignition advance and fires the coil. At high engine speed the same angle arrives sooner, so the sampling period must shrink. Coil and injector delays shift the spark; crank-sensor error shifts it too, causing knock or a misfire.

ABS is a clear CPS. A tone ring with fixed teeth turns with each wheel. The sensor produces pulses; the controller computes wheel speed and wheel slip. It then commands brake-pressure valves. The sampling period must be short enough to catch a locking wheel, the valve delay limits how fast pressure can fall, and tooth or gap error adds speed error.

EBD uses the same ABS sensors to split braking force between axles. Adaptive cruise control measures the gap to the car ahead and commands throttle or brakes. In both, the loop is closed, so the values above set the physical result.

A drone is a CPS with fast inner loops. An inertial measurement unit (IMU) measures rotation rate and acceleration. A controller compares the desired attitude with the measured attitude and sets motor speeds. Electronic speed controllers drive the motors and propellers. Only a few syllabi teach the drone control equations; know the blocks: estimate, compare, command, actuate, measure again. IMU sampling must be fast, motor and propeller delay must be small, and vibration causes sensor error.

An autonomous robot adds a vision system. A camera produces frames; vision code finds an obstacle or a lane; a planner sets wheel speeds. The camera sampling period is longer than the wheel-control period. The robot must handle that delay. Lighting changes and lens dirt are sensor errors; wheel slip and motor lag are actuator delays.

A robotic camera dolly is a small CPS used in video. An encoder measures wheel position; a controller drives the motor to follow a planned move. Smooth motion needs short sampling and low actuator delay. Encoder error or a late motor command makes the move jerky, and a jerky dolly blurs the shot.

figure.caption: The loop measures wheel state, computes a brake command and applies torque. Notice the return edge: braking changes the wheel that the sensor measures.

spec.title: CPS feedback loop
spec.aria: A cyber-physical system measures a physical process, computes a command and drives actuators that change the process, closing the loop.

examples.question: An ABS wheel has radius 0.32 m and a 48-tooth tone ring. The car moves at 60 km/h. Find the wheel angular speed in rad/s, the wheel revolutions per second, and the pulse frequency from the ABS sensor. Use π = 3.1416.
steps: Wheel angular speed: ω = v ÷ r = 16.67 ÷ 0.32 = 52.08 rad/s.
Revolutions per second: n = ω ÷ 2π = 52.08 ÷ 6.2832 = 8.29 rev/s.
Pulse frequency: f = n × teeth = 8.29 × 48 = 397.9 Hz.
examples.answer: Converting 60 km/h gives 16.67 m/s; the wheel turns at 52.08 rad/s (8.29 rev/s) and the tone ring gives 397.9 pulses per second.
examples.check:
import math
v = 60 / 3.6
r = 0.32
omega = v / r
rev = omega / (2 * math.pi)
freq = rev * 48
print(round(v, 2))
print(round(omega, 2))
print(round(rev, 2))
print(round(freq, 1))

traps: Do not put km/h into v = ωr. Convert to m/s first: 60 km/h = 16.67 m/s.
The 48 teeth are per wheel revolution, not per second of travel. Multiply rev/s by 48, not speed by 48.
Sampling period T<sub>s</sub> and sampling frequency f<sub>s</sub> are inverses. A 10 ms period is 100 Hz, not 10 Hz.
Sensor error is a wrong measurement. Actuator delay is a late action. One does not fix the other.
A CPS needs a closed loop. A sensor that only sends data to a dashboard is monitoring, not closed-loop control.

quiz.q: Define sampling period and actuator delay in a CPS.
quiz.a: Sampling period T<sub>s</sub> is the time between two measurements in seconds. Actuator delay is the time from a command to its physical effect.

quiz.q: Why can a CPS with correct code still give a wrong physical result?
quiz.a: Code can be correct but late. Slow sampling misses a fast change, actuator delay makes a correction late, and sensor error makes a correction wrong. The closed loop turns these into physical error.

quiz.q: A wheel has radius 0.25 m and a 36-tooth tone ring. The car moves at 36 km/h. Find the ABS pulse frequency.
A drone is stable at low speed but oscillates at high speed. Use sampling and actuator delay to explain.
quiz.a: At high speed the physical state changes faster. The same IMU sampling period and motor delay become a larger fraction of the loop time. The correction arrives late, so the controller overshoots and oscillates. A faster loop or lower delay is needed.

quiz.q: Give one sensor error and one actuator delay in ABS.
quiz.a: A dirty or damaged tone ring gives a wrong wheel-speed pulse: sensor error. A brake valve that takes time to release pressure is actuator delay.

quiz.q: A camera dolly has a 1000-count-per-revolution encoder on a wheel of radius 0.05 m. It must move at 0.2 m/s. Find the encoder count rate.
quiz.a: Wheel circumference = 2π × 0.05 = 0.3142 m. Wheel rev/s = 0.2 ÷ 0.3142 = 0.6366. Count rate = 0.6366 × 1000 = 636.6 counts/s.

quiz.q: Why is ABS a cyber-physical system and not just a sensor system?
quiz.a: ABS measures wheel speed, computes slip and commands brake pressure in a loop. The actuator changes the wheel, and the next measurement depends on that change. The physical braking result depends on loop timing.

beyond: Not for the exam. In industry, CPS work uses real-time operating systems, hardware-in-the-loop test rigs and sensor fusion. Robot middleware such as ROS 2 separates sensing, planning and actuation with timing contracts. Newer curricula connect CPS to digital twins and industrial edge control. Search next for real-time control, sensor fusion, hardware-in-the-loop and robot middleware.
